title: Electron transfer reactions
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for IB Diploma Chemistry (status of the source: ai-reviewed-reverified-gate-verified-2026-09-30-awaiting-human-signoff). Terms and clues: R3.2#c02 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; R3.2.9#xt1 term and clue written for the game; R3.2.9#xt2 term and clue written for the game; R3.2.3#xt1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: R3.2#q17, R3.2#q19, R3.2#q22, R3.2#q25, R3.2#q18, R3.2#q20, R3.2#q23, R3.2#q39, R3.2#q21, R3.2#q24, R3.2#q38, R3.2#q26, R3.2#q31, R3.2#q33, R3.2#q32, R3.2#q42.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Reduction
items.clue: Gain of electrons by a species, shown by a decrease in the oxidation state of an element.

items.label: Reflux
items.clue: Heating with a vertical condenser so vapour returns to the flask; gives the carboxylic acid.

items.label: Distillation
items.clue: Collecting the aldehyde as it vaporizes from the mixture, before it can be oxidized further.

items.label: Displacement reaction
items.clue: A metal that is more easily oxidized reduces the aqueous ions of another metal, depositing it.

questions.stem: Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed using graphite electrodes. How is the electric current conducted through the molten lead(II) bromide itself?

options.text: By electrons moving through the melt from the cathode to the anode
By Pb²⁺ and Br⁻ ions, already present, moving to the electrodes
By delocalized electrons released when the solid melts
By ions that the current creates by splitting up the lead(II) bromide

questions.explanation: Lead(II) bromide consists of ions. Melting frees them to move: Pb²⁺ moves to the cathode and Br⁻ to the anode. Electrons carry the current only in the wires and electrodes.

questions.stem: Butan-1-ol is converted into butanoic acid by heating it under reflux with an acidified oxidizing agent. Why is reflux used?

options.text: Reflux removes butanal from the flask as soon as it has formed.
Reflux converts butan-1-ol straight to the acid, with no butanal formed.
Reflux keeps air in contact with the mixture so its oxygen can react.
Reflux returns condensed vapour, so butanal stays in the flask to be oxidized.

questions.explanation: The vertical condenser returns volatile butanal (formed in the first step) to the flask, where it is oxidized further to butanoic acid.

questions.stem: Butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃, is reduced. What is the organic product?

options.text: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH
CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃
CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃
CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH

questions.explanation: Reduction adds hydrogen to the C=O carbon and oxygen of the ketone. The OH stays on carbon 2, so the product is the secondary alcohol butan-2-ol.

questions.stem: Hex-1-en-5-yne, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₂C≡CH, reacts completely with excess hydrogen in the presence of a nickel catalyst. What amount of H₂ reacts with 1 mol of hex-1-en-5-yne?

options.text: 2 mol
5 mol
6 mol
3 mol

questions.explanation: The C=C bond takes 1 mol of H₂ and the C≡C bond takes 2 mol, giving hexane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃. Total 3 mol.

questions.stem: Molten potassium iodide, KI(l), is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Which half-equation shows the reaction at the anode?

options.text: 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻
2I⁻ + 2e⁻ → I₂

questions.explanation: The anode is where oxidation occurs. The only anion in the melt is I⁻, which loses electrons to form iodine.

questions.stem: 2-methylpropan-2-ol, (CH₃)₃COH, is heated with an acidified oxidizing agent under the conditions that oxidize ethanol. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It is oxidized to a ketone, as its OH group is on a central carbon.
It is oxidized to a carboxylic acid if it is heated for long enough.
It is not oxidized, as its C–OH carbon carries no hydrogen atom.
It is not oxidized, as only primary alcohols can be oxidized.

questions.explanation: (CH₃)₃COH is a tertiary alcohol: the carbon bearing the OH is bonded to three carbons and no hydrogen, so it cannot be oxidized under these conditions.

questions.stem: Carbonyl compounds are reduced by reducing agents that act as a source of hydride ions, H⁻. What is the role of the hydride ion?

options.text: It adds hydrogen to the carbon of the C=O group, so the compound is reduced.
It removes hydrogen from the carbonyl compound, which reduces the compound.
It acts as an acid, donating a proton, H⁺, to the oxygen of the C=O group.
It is a catalyst, written above the arrow as it is not used up in the reaction.

questions.explanation: The hydride ion supplies hydrogen, with an electron pair, to the carbonyl carbon. The organic compound gains hydrogen, which is reduction.

questions.stem: Oct-4-yne, CH₃CH₂CH₂C≡CCH₂CH₂CH₃, reacts completely with excess hydrogen in the presence of a nickel catalyst. What is the organic product?

options.text: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH=CHCH₂CH₂CH₃
CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃
CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ and CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃
CH₃CH₂CH₂CHOHCHOHCH₂CH₂CH₃

questions.explanation: The C≡C bond has two π bonds, and each takes one H₂. With excess hydrogen both are hydrogenated, so the triple bond becomes a single bond and the product is the saturated alkane octane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ (C₈H₁₈).

questions.stem: Propan-1-ol is heated under reflux with an excess of acidified oxidizing agent, represented by [O]. Which equation represents the overall change?

options.text: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃COCH₃ + H₂O
CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃CH₂CHO + H₂O
CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + 9[O] → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O
CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + 2[O] → CH₃CH₂COOH + H₂O

questions.explanation: Under reflux both steps occur: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃CH₂CHO + H₂O, then CH₃CH₂CHO + [O] → CH₃CH₂COOH. Overall, two [O] are used and propanoic acid forms.

questions.stem: Which describes the reduction of propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH?

options.text: Propan-1-ol forms in a single step, with no aldehyde formed.
Propanal forms first and is then reduced to propan-1-ol.
Propanone forms first and is then reduced to propan-2-ol.
Propane forms, as reduction removes both of its oxygen atoms.

questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids are reduced to primary alcohols via the aldehyde: CH₃CH₂COOH → CH₃CH₂CHO → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH.

questions.stem: Propan-1-ol is heated with an acidified oxidizing agent in apparatus set up for distillation, and the distillate is collected. What is the main organic product collected, and why?

options.text: Propanoic acid, as distillation keeps propanal in the flask
Propanone, as the alcohol is oxidized to a ketone
Propanal, as it distils out before it can be oxidized further
Propanoic acid, as it forms directly in one step

questions.explanation: The first step gives propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO, which is more volatile than the alcohol and the acid. In distillation the vapour passes into the condenser and is collected elsewhere, so propanal leaves the flask before it can be oxidized to propanoic acid.

questions.stem: Why is the standard electrode potential of the hydrogen half-cell, H⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ ½H₂(g), given as 0 V?

options.text: It is assigned by convention as the reference for other half-cells.
No oxidation or reduction occurs at the hydrogen electrode.
Its absolute potential has been measured directly and found to be zero.
The platinum electrode is inert, so no potential develops.

questions.explanation: Only potential differences can be measured, so one half-cell must be chosen as the reference and given a value. By convention it is the standard hydrogen electrode, set at 0 V.

questions.stem: CuSO₄(aq) is electrolysed first with graphite electrodes and then with copper electrodes. Which statement explains the difference at the anode?

options.text: With copper electrodes, the anode itself is oxidized to Cu²⁺, so no oxygen forms.
There is no difference: water is oxidized to oxygen at both types of anode.
With copper electrodes, Cu²⁺ ions are reduced to copper at the anode.
With graphite electrodes, sulfate ions are oxidized at the anode, not water.

questions.stem: A steel key is electroplated with copper using a copper anode and CuSO₄(aq) as the electrolyte. Which half-equation shows the reaction at the key?

options.text: Cu(s) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻
Cu²⁺(aq) → Cu(s) + 2e⁻
Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s)

questions.explanation: The key is the cathode. Electrons supplied by the power source reduce Cu²⁺ ions to copper, which coats the key. At the copper anode, Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ replaces the ions.

questions.stem: When water is electrolysed, a little sulfuric acid is usually added. Hydrogen forms at the cathode and oxygen at the anode. What is the role of the sulfuric acid?

options.text: It is the source of the hydrogen and oxygen gases produced.
It supplies ions so that the water conducts a useful current.
It lets electrons travel through the water between the electrodes.
It lets the current split the water into ions that carry charge.

questions.explanation: Pure water contains very few ions and conducts poorly. The added ions carry the current; water is decomposed at the electrodes, 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂, and the acid is not used up.

questions.stem: A steel bracelet is to be electroplated with silver. It is placed in AgNO₃(aq) with a silver rod as the second electrode; the bracelet is connected to the negative terminal of a DC power supply and the silver rod to the positive terminal. Which statement about this cell is correct?

options.text: The silver rod is the cathode, because Ag⁺(aq) ions are produced at it
The bracelet is the anode, because it is connected to the negative terminal
Water is oxidized to O₂(g) at the silver rod, which only conducts the current
The silver rod is the anode and dissolves, forming Ag⁺(aq) ions
